knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Its relationship to the strategic principle of two weaknesses is a genuine structural link, not an analogy of convenience.
definition_short: A piece with two defensive jobs cannot do both; take one and the other collapses.
definition_long:
A single unit is the only defender of two things. The tactic exploits the fact that answering one threat abandons the other. It is listed as a category in the Encyclopedia of Chess Middlegames.

Overloading is the tactical form of the same logic that the PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES applies strategically: finite defensive resources stretched across more duties than they can cover. The difference is timescale — overloading resolves in a move or two, two weaknesses over dozens.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: One enemy unit is the sole defender of two distinct targets or duties
indicators_for: Removing or diverting that unit leaves both targets loose
The two duties require the piece to be on different squares
indicators_against: A second defender covers one of the duties
The piece can perform both duties from one square
Capturing the overloaded piece is answered by a recapture that restores the defence

exceptions: A defender that appears overloaded may be adequate if one 'duty' was never real.
limitations: Depends on enumerating duties, which is a functional judgement.

by_level.beginner: That piece is guarding two things at once. Take one and it cannot keep guarding the other.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} is overloaded — it is the only defender of both {a} and {b}.
by_level.advanced: Overloading. The tactical counterpart of the principle of two weaknesses: the same finite-defence logic on a shorter timescale.
